title: Rome under Constantine, c. 315 CE
text: In 315 Constantine dedicated his triumphal arch beside the Colosseum after defeating Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge (312). The Basilica of Maxentius was completed under his name, the Forum, the imperial fora, temples and baths were maintained and in daily use. Rome was still the largest city of the Mediterranean.
source: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City; Lenski (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to the Age of Constantine

title: Size of the city in the Regionary Catalogues
text: The fourth-century Regionary Catalogues (Notitia and Curiosum urbis Romae) list for the fourteen regions about 46,602 insulae (apartment blocks), 1,790 domus (private houses), 290 horrea (warehouses), 856 small baths and 254 bakeries. Modern estimates of the population range from 700,000 to about one million.
source: Notitia urbis Romae / Curiosum urbis Romae (c. 315-357 CE); Storey, 'The population of ancient Rome', Antiquity 71 (1997)

title: The toga and the senatorial stripe
text: The toga was the formal garment of male citizens: a large semicircle of white wool draped over the left shoulder, under the right arm and back over the left. Senators wore beneath it a tunic with a broad purple stripe (latus clavus) running from each shoulder; equestrians wore narrow stripes (angustus clavus). Magistrates and free-born boys wore the toga praetexta with a purple border. Senators wore red shoes (calcei mullei).
source: Sebesta & Bonfante (eds.), The World of Roman Costume (1994); Croom, Roman Clothing and Fashion (2010)

title: Everyday dress of ordinary men
text: Most men in the street wore a knee-length belted wool tunic, often undyed in natural cream, brown or grey, or dyed with cheap dyes: madder (red), woad (blue), weld (yellow). By the fourth century long-sleeved tunics decorated with woven bands (clavi) and roundels (orbiculi) were common. Workers and slaves wore the exomis, a tunic fastened on one shoulder leaving the right arm free.
source: Croom, Roman Clothing and Fashion (2010); Late antique tunics from Egypt, Metropolitan Museum collection

title: Dress of women
text: Married citizen women (matronae) wore the stola, a long sleeveless overdress worn over a tunic, and the palla, a large mantle wrapped around the body and drawn over the head in public. Rich women wore coloured silks and wool dyed with expensive purples and saffron yellow, with jewellery and elaborate hair. Working women wore long tunics and a shawl.
source: Olson, Dress and the Roman Woman (2008); Sebesta, 'Symbolism in the costume of the Roman woman'

title: Cloaks for rain and cold
text: In bad weather Romans wore the paenula, a heavy hooded cape of thick wool or leather closed at the front, and the lacerna, an open cloak pinned at the shoulder. The cucullus was a separate hood. Travellers and workers wore felt caps (pilleus) and broad hats (petasus).
source: Croom, Roman Clothing and Fashion (2010); Juvenal, Satires; Martial, Epigrams XIV

title: Purple dye
text: True purple from murex sea snails was the most expensive dye of antiquity and a sign of rank; imperial purple was restricted to the emperor. Cheaper imitations used madder and woad. Bright colours were a sign of wealth; undyed wool was the colour of the poor.
source: Pliny the Elder, Natural History IX.60-65; Reinhold, History of Purple as a Status Symbol in Antiquity (1970)

title: Soldiers in the city
text: Constantine disbanded the Praetorian Guard in 312. The city was policed by the urban cohorts (cohortes urbanae) under the urban prefect. Fourth-century soldiers wore mail or scale armour over a long-sleeved tunic, trousers, ridge helmets and carried oval shields and spears.
source: Southern & Dixon, The Late Roman Army (1996); Zosimus II.17

title: Vigiles — the night watch
text: Seven cohorts of vigiles, about 3,500 freedmen, served as firemen and night watchmen, one cohort for every two regions, with stations (excubitoria). They patrolled at night with lamps and torches, carried buckets, axes and ropes, and could arrest thieves.
source: Rainbird, 'The fire stations of imperial Rome', PBSR 54 (1986); Digest I.15

title: Children
text: Free-born children wore a small tunic and the bulla, an amulet locket hung round the neck, which boys dedicated when they took the adult toga at about 15. Children worked, ran errands and played games in the streets and porticoes.
source: Rawson, Children and Childhood in Roman Italy (2003)

title: Vestal Virgins
text: The six Vestal Virgins tended the sacred fire in the round Temple of Vesta in the Forum and lived in the Atrium Vestae beside it. They wore white, with the infula headband and the suffibulum, a white veil fastened with a brooch, and were among the few women allowed a lictor and a carriage in the city.
source: Wildfang, Rome's Vestal Virgins (2006)

title: Litters and bearers
text: The wealthy travelled through the crowded streets in a lectica, a covered couch with curtains carried on poles by four to eight bearers (lecticarii), often slaves chosen for height and dressed in matching tunics. The sella was a carried chair. At night torchbearers walked ahead of litters.
source: Juvenal, Satire III; Martial; Seneca, Letters; Croom, Running the Roman Home

title: Wheeled traffic and the Lex Julia
text: A law of Caesar's time (Lex Julia municipalis, Tabula Heracleensis) banned wagons from the streets of Rome for the first ten hours after sunrise, except carts carrying material for temples and public works, removing demolition rubble, and ceremonial vehicles. Heavy goods therefore entered the city at dusk and through the night, and Juvenal complains that the rumbling carts made sleep impossible.
source: Tabula Heracleensis lines 56-67 (CIL I2 593); Juvenal, Satire III.236-238

title: Carts and draught animals
text: The plaustrum was a heavy two- or four-wheeled cart with solid wheels pulled by oxen; lighter carts (carrus, carpentum) were drawn by mules or donkeys. They carried grain, wine and oil amphorae, building stone, timber, bricks and firewood. Donkeys with panniers and porters carried goods by day.
source: Raepsaet, 'Land transport', in Oxford Handbook of Engineering and Technology in the Classical World (2008)

title: Boats on the Tiber
text: Goods arriving at Ostia and Portus were transferred to river barges (naves caudicariae) that were towed upstream by oxen or men along a towpath, about three days to Rome. Smaller boats (lintres) and ferries crossed the river. The river port, Portus Tiberinus, lay beside the Forum Boarium, and the great Emporium with the Porticus Aemilia lay downstream below the Aventine.
source: Casson, Ships and Seamanship in the Ancient World; Aldrete, Floods of the Tiber in Ancient Rome (2007); Malmberg, 'Navigating the urban Via Tiberina'

title: Markets of the city
text: Food was sold in specialised markets: the Forum Boarium (cattle), the Forum Holitorium (vegetables), the Forum Piscarium (fish), the Forum Cuppedinis (delicacies) and great covered markets (macella) such as the Macellum Magnum on the Caelian and the Macellum Liviae. Trajan's Markets held shops and offices. Periodic markets (nundinae) were held every eighth day.
source: De Ruyt, Macellum: marché alimentaire des Romains (1983); Holleran, Shopping in Ancient Rome (2012)

title: Shops and street trade
text: Ground floors of insulae were lined with tabernae: single-room shops with a wide opening and a masonry counter, where bakers, fullers, wine sellers, cooks and craftsmen worked. Pedlars, hawkers and money-changers worked in the porticoes, and stalls spilled into the street until Domitian's edict cleared them.
source: Holleran, Shopping in Ancient Rome (2012); Martial VII.61

title: The Roman day
text: The day was divided into twelve hours from sunrise to sunset. Clients visited their patrons at dawn (salutatio); business, courts and markets filled the morning; work stopped around the sixth or seventh hour (noon) for a light meal and rest; the afternoon belonged to the baths, exercise and leisure; the main meal (cena) began in the late afternoon. After dark the streets were unlit and dangerous except for the carts.
source: Carcopino, Daily Life in Ancient Rome; Martial IV.8

title: Streets and paving
text: Major streets inside the city were paved with large polygonal blocks of grey-black basalt (silex) laid tightly on a gravel bed, with raised sidewalks (crepidines) and stepping stones in places. Smaller lanes (vici, semitae) were narrow, often unpaved or cobbled, and climbed the hills with steps (scalae, gradus).
source: Vitruvius VII.1; Laurence, Roads of Roman Italy (1999); van Tilburg, Traffic and Congestion in the Roman Empire (2007)

title: Lighting after dark
text: Rome had no street lighting. Light came from oil lamps in windows and shops, lanterns (laternae) of horn or glass carried by walkers, torches carried by slaves ahead of their masters and by the vigiles, and the fires of the night carts. Shrines at crossroads (compita) sometimes had lamps.
source: Ellis, 'Lighting in the streets of Roman cities'; Juvenal III.268-301

title: Climate of Rome
text: Rome has a Mediterranean climate: hot dry summers (June-August) and mild wet winters; most rain falls from October to April, in autumn often as heavy showers and thunderstorms. Morning mists form over the Tiber valley in autumn and winter. Snow is rare but recorded in ancient sources in cold winters, usually lying only briefly.
source: Aldrete, Floods of the Tiber in Ancient Rome (2007); Livy V.13 and XXI.62; modern climatology of Rome

title: Floods of the Tiber
text: The Tiber flooded the low-lying Campus Martius, Velabrum and Forum Boarium many times, usually after heavy winter and spring rains. The curators of the Tiber banks (curatores alvei Tiberis) maintained the embankments and boundary stones along the river.
source: Aldrete, Floods of the Tiber in Ancient Rome (2007)

title: Colour of the city
text: Temples were faced with white Luna and Greek marbles, with painted details and gilded bronze roof tiles on the greatest temples (Jupiter Capitolinus, Venus and Roma). Public buildings showed brick-faced concrete covered with stucco and marble veneer. Insulae were of brick and concrete, often plastered and painted in ochre and red, with red tiled roofs and wooden balconies (maeniana).
source: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide; Packer, The Insulae of Imperial Ostia

title: Gardens and trees
text: The city was ringed with great gardens (horti) of the rich, and porticoes such as the Porticus Liviae and the Temple of Peace had planted courts. Plane trees, laurel, myrtle, box, cypress and stone pines were favoured; vines and fruit trees grew in courtyards.
source: Jashemski, The Gardens of Pompeii; Farrar, Ancient Roman Gardens (1998); Pliny, Natural History XII

title: Animals in the streets
text: Mules, donkeys and oxen pulled carts and turned mills; dogs guarded houses (cave canem); cattle, sheep and pigs were driven to the Forum Boarium and the slaughterers; pigs were brought from southern Italy for the free pork ration introduced by Aurelian.
source: MacKinnon, Production and Consumption of Animals in Roman Italy (2004); Codex Theodosianus XIV.4
